rv.q: If you’re feeling the autumn blues, seize your straw boater immediately and head to Kingston for this gorgeous burst of theatrical sunshine.
This is a vivid, panto-adjacent romp that delivers a huge dose of feelgood fun and a couple of moments of genuine pathos.
Despite two-and-a-half hours of digressions, the story still remains buoyant.
Slapstick dominates in an engaging evening that smooths the jagged oddness of the book.
It’s fun at first, but you can’t sustain nearly three hours of theatre on patter, strolling songs and knob gags.
Following three friends and a dog as they take a calamitous boat trip up the Thames from Kingston to Oxford, Al Smith’s madcap new version is stupendously silly and full of frivolous fun.

It truly is an excellent show, and this was presented in the standing ovation given by the audience at the end of Wednesday's performance - I would highly recommend that if you have not yet seen the production; buy a ticket asap.
Three Men in a Boat is quite close to a comedic masterpiece that shines in every aspect – music, stage design, direction, puppetry and, of course, comedy.

The Rose Theatre’s new production of Three Men in a Boat takes Jerome K. Jerome’s much-loved comic novel and sends it hurtling down the Thames in a wonderfully silly, energetic and frequently hilarious adventure.

Three Men in a Boat is a joyful couple of hours of late summer fun: get yourself to Kingston and revel in it as this lengthy summer continues, and delight in the combination of clever acting, skilled direction and impressive stagecraft.
Smith’s lighthearted adaptation, tightly directed by the Rose’s artistic director Christopher Haydon, is a riot of music hall styling, strong physical comedy and broad satire.
A quintessential British comedy with strong performances, an excellent script and jokes galore, it's a guaranteed fun trip to the theatre.
Three Men in a Boat is full of mischief and eccentricity.
Funny, energetic and winningly performed, this busy adaptation loses its way whenever it reaches for insights beyond Jerome K. Jerome’s timeless original.
I really wanted to love this show and perhaps my expectations were always too high.

"This mangled mess at the delightful Rose Theatre" "For all the energy of the company, and I do not criticise them as being responsible for this compendium of unfunny physical comedy and jokes, some anachronistic with fourth wall breaches, the incomprehensible narrative, and forced humour this boat is holed beneath the waterline and sank with...
This is one trip up the Thames you won’t regret making.
For me, this was a brilliantly bonkers night a t the theatre, a chaotic stag do on the Thames that goes a bout a s wrong a s it possibly can, while somehow getting everything right.

cn.t: This madcap adaptation of Jerome K. Jerome's classic novel divides critics with its chaotic energy and silly humor. Most praise the riotous fun and strong performances, though some find it an overstuffed mess that loses the original's gentle charm.
